ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a circuit in which an AC power source controls a resistive load through a bidirectional thyristor triac. The power source is labeled v_s = 230√2 sin(ωt), the firing angle is labeled α = π/4, and the load is a pure resistor, labeled R = 10 Ω. Reasoning: For a pure resistive load, the triac conducts in the positive half-cycle from α to π, and conducts symmetrically in the negative half-cycle; when conducting, the load voltage equals the source voltage. Since α = π/4 < π/2, the source voltage peak value 230√2 will appear within the conduction interval. Therefore the load peak power is P_peak = V_peak^2 / R = (230√2)^2 / 10 = 10580 W.

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: Direct instantaneous-power route using the peak of the conducted sinusoid; this is the natural single solution for the problem.
planner_metadata.image_role: Read the circuit diagram: a triac in series with a purely resistive load labeled R = 10 Ω, supplied by an AC source labeled 230√2 sin(ωt), with firing angle α = π/4.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question text only to identify that the requested quantity is the peak power dissipation in the resistive load of the shown triac circuit.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: For an ideal triac feeding a resistive load, once fired it applies the source voltage to the load during the conducting part of each half-cycle. Instantaneous load power is p(t)=v_L(t)^2/R. Peak dissipation is the maximum of this expression over the conduction interval; since α=π/4 is before π/2, the sinusoidal voltage peak occurs while conducting.
